title: Making old weather records usable
content:
At a regional records centre, a collection of weather registers has become a test of what digitisation can reasonably promise. The registers were written by observers who recorded conditions beside their ordinary work at farms, schools and small ports. Researchers want to compare observations across places and years, but the centre also serves local people who value the books as objects. A readable image is therefore only one product of the project. Information about where a register came from, how it was arranged and which pages have been altered matters as much as the speed with which a visitor can retrieve a temperature.

Before a register reaches the camera, a conservator examines its binding and records damage on an assessment sheet. Pages with active mould are isolated; photographing them immediately would risk carrying contamination into the shared workspace. Loose surface dirt is removed with a soft brush when the paper is strong enough to tolerate it. Staff do not attempt to make every page look new. A stain may obscure a measurement, but removing it could also disturb an entry or eliminate evidence of how the book was used. Decisions about treatment are recorded rather than concealed in a polished final image.

The camera station is designed around the book instead of requiring the book to lie flat. A padded cradle supports bindings that cannot safely open all the way. Staff adjust the camera position and lighting before beginning a volume, then keep the arrangement stable while taking the images. At the start of each session, they photograph a colour target alongside the register. This reference helps later users distinguish a change in the paper from a change in the lighting. It does not allow them to reconstruct a colour that the original photograph failed to capture.

Images are assigned filenames from a persistent identifier and a page sequence. The identifier follows the physical register even if a catalogue description changes. A small card is inserted temporarily when a leaf is missing so that a sequence of images cannot silently suggest that the text is complete. The main image is stored as a TIFF file; the public website displays a smaller derivative. Researchers can request the larger file, but routine browsing does not require transferring every detail preserved in the master image. Keeping the two versions separate also lets the centre replace its website without photographing the books again.

Turning handwriting into searchable data introduces a different kind of uncertainty. A transcription program offers suggestions, but a human reader reviews each page. When a second reader cannot resolve a disputed figure, the entry is marked uncertain instead of being replaced by the value that seems most plausible. The original mark remains visible through a link from the data table to the image. This matters because an unusual temperature could be a copying error, an instrument fault or a genuine event. Correcting every unusual value would make the series tidier while possibly removing the observations that a researcher most needs to investigate.

The centre uses two distinct checks before releasing a batch. A sequence check looks for missing or repeated page images. A checksum is then calculated for each master file so that later changes to the stored data can be detected. The checksum cannot show whether a page was photographed sharply, so staff also inspect sample images at full size. A copy is held at a second site, and restoration is tested rather than assumed to work. These procedures address different failures: an intact backup of a blurred photograph still contains a blurred photograph.

Access remains a continuing task after the first release. Visitors can suggest corrections without editing the master transcription directly, and accepted changes retain a record of the previous reading. The centre keeps physical volumes available by appointment because some questions involve bindings, watermarks or the order in which entries were added. Digital access can reduce routine handling, but it does not remove the need to preserve the objects. The project is successful when it makes the records easier to use while keeping uncertainty and editorial intervention visible.
